_work.title: Qur'at al-Khulafa' al-Abbasiyya — Oracle of the Abbasid Caliphs (Princeton, Garrett no. 551Hq)
_work.blurb: An oversize Arabic divination manuscript, 38 leaves (80 pages), held at Princeton University Library (Oversize Islamic Manuscripts, Garrett no. 551Hq). The Qur'at al-Khulafa' al-Abbasiyya Umara' al-Mu'minin (Oracle/Lottery of the Abbasid Caliphs, Commanders of the Faithful) is a systematic oracle book organized around the Abbasid Caliphs — each Caliph providing a set of verse-predictions in a two-column format for different query types. The MS is visually extraordinary: it contains seven full-page illuminated concentric-ring circle diagrams (dawa'ir) labeled by topic — Caliphs, Tribes, Women, Turks, Birds, Cities — and a grid page showing eight smaller oracle circles. These circles function as divinatory instruments: the querent follows a procedure involving letters and numbers (via the Zairja or qur'a system) to arrive at a specific cell in the concentric rings, which then directs them to the appropriate Caliph oracle section. Each circle has a gold or blue-grey decorative background in the outer ring, with alternating red and black Arabic text in the inner rings, and decorative cloud-curl corner ornaments. The combination of Islamic calligraphy, geometric diagrammatic precision, and cosmological structure makes these circles among the most visually striking Islamic divination diagrams in any collection.
_work.rights: Public Domain — Islamic manuscript, 1700-1835 CE. Princeton University Library (Garrett Collection).
_work.creator: Anonymous

entries.title: Title Page — Inverted Triangle Text Block (Qur'at al-Khulafa', p. 5)
entries.rights: Public Domain. Princeton University Library (Garrett Collection).
entries.summary: The title page of the Qur'at al-Khulafa' al-Abbasiyya, featuring the work's title arranged in an inverted-triangle (or 'mukhamas'/pentagonal) text block — lines of Arabic text that decrease in length from top to bottom, forming a downward-pointing triangular visual form. The title reads 'Hadhihi Qur'at al-Khulafa' al-Abbasiyya Umara' al-Mu'minin' (This is the Oracle of the Abbasid Caliphs, Commanders of the Faithful). This geometric text arrangement — where the content and the visual form coincide — is a distinctively Islamic calligraphic practice; the triangle or inverted-triangle poem is one of several visual poem types (shi'r mushakkal) used in Islamic manuscripts for titles, dedications, and opening verses. The result is a page that is simultaneously text and diagram, in the tradition of lettrism where the visual shape of written language carries meaning alongside its semantic content.

entries.title: Eight Oracle Circles Grid (Dawa'ir al-Su'al) — Qur'at al-Khulafa' (p. 7)
entries.medium: manuscript, ink on paper, gold ground
entries.rights: Public Domain. Princeton University Library (Garrett Collection).
entries.summary: A spectacular full-page diagram from the Qur'at al-Khulafa' showing eight small concentric-ring oracle circles arranged in a 2×4 grid, against a gold/brown decorative background with blue floral ornament at center and white cloud-curl corner decorations. The page heading reads 'Hadhihi Dawa'ir al-Su'al al-Thani li-Ikhraj al-Damir' (These are the circles of the second question for extracting the hidden [answer]). Each of the eight circles contains concentric rings of Arabic text — the same structure as the large full-page circles, but here compressed to a small size — likely representing eight different query categories or eight stages of the divination procedure. The gold background and blue ornamental motif create a page that looks like an illuminated manuscript folio: the eight-circle grid format transforms the divinatory instrument into a visual composition. In the Islamic qur'a tradition, these concentric-ring circles encode the numerical/letter relationships that allow the practitioner to navigate from a query (a word, a letter, a number) through a series of rings to an answer cell, which then directs them to the appropriate Caliph oracle verse.

entries.title: Circle of the Lunar Mansions (Al-Dairat al-Thaniya) — Qur'at al-Khulafa' (p. 9)
entries.rights: Public Domain. Princeton University Library (Garrett Collection).
entries.summary: A full-page concentric-ring circle from the Qur'at al-Khulafa', labeled 'Al-Dairat al-Thaniya li-Jam' al-Huruf wa-Ma'rifat al-Manazil' (The Second Circle for Combining Letters and Knowing the [Lunar] Mansions). The outermost ring shows the 28 lunar mansions (manazil al-qamar) of Arabic astronomical tradition — names like al-Thuraya (the Pleiades), al-Dabaraan (Aldebaran), al-Haqa, al-Han'a, al-Dhira', etc. — the 28 stations of the Moon that divide the zodiac in the Arabic/Islamic system. Inner rings contain additional text relating the mansions to letter combinations and divinatory outcomes. The 28 lunar mansions are fundamental to Islamic cosmological and divinatory tradition: each mansion governs a day of the lunar month, a set of activities (favorable or unfavorable), a planet, an element, and a letter of the alphabet — making them the operational interface between astronomical observation and practical divination. This circle visually encodes that entire system in a single diagrammatic form.

entries.title: Dairat al-Khulafa' (Circle of the Caliphs) — Qur'at al-Khulafa' (p. 17)
entries.medium: manuscript, ink on paper, blue-grey ground
entries.rights: Public Domain. Princeton University Library (Garrett Collection).
entries.summary: A full-page illuminated concentric-ring circle from the Qur'at al-Khulafa', titled 'Hadhihi Dairat al-Khulafa' [bi-ism] Allah Ta'ala' (This is the Circle of the Caliphs [in the name of] God Most High). The circle has a blue-grey decorative background in the outer square frame, with white cloud-curl ornaments in the four corners — a different color scheme from the gold-ground circles, suggesting a section transition. The concentric rings contain the names of the Abbasid Caliphs in alternating red and black ink, organized so that each ring corresponds to a different category of query, and the Caliphs listed in each cell direct the querent to the appropriate oracle section for their answer. The Caliph circle is the primary navigation diagram of the entire work: it encodes the relationship between the query type (what you are asking about) and the Caliph oracle (which set of verse predictions to consult). The blue-grey background with gold text-ring gives this page a cooler, more formal visual tone than the warm gold circles.

entries.title: Dairat al-Qaba'il (Circle of the Tribes) — Qur'at al-Khulafa' (p. 21)
entries.medium: manuscript, ink on paper, gold ground
entries.rights: Public Domain. Princeton University Library (Garrett Collection).
entries.summary: A full-page illuminated concentric-ring circle titled 'Hadhihi Dairat al-Qaba'il' (This is the Circle of the Tribes) from the Qur'at al-Khulafa'. The outer square background is gold/brown, the corner ornaments are white cloud-curls, and the concentric rings contain Arabic tribal names and associated verse-directives in alternating red and black ink. In the Qur'a system, 'tribes' (qaba'il) is a query category: questions about inter-tribal relations, blood feuds, genealogy, alliance formation, and collective identity are routed to this circle, which then directs the querent to the appropriate Caliph oracle section. The circle of tribes reflects the deep relevance of tribal identity in Arabic poetry and culture — the Abbasid-era poets whose oracles fill the MS were all identified with specific tribal affiliations, and the oracle system itself is structured around the social categories of pre-Islamic and early Islamic Arab society.

entries.title: Dairat al-Nisa' (Circle of Women) — Qur'at al-Khulafa' (p. 24)
entries.medium: manuscript, ink on paper, dark ground
entries.rights: Public Domain. Princeton University Library (Garrett Collection).
entries.summary: A full-page illuminated concentric-ring circle titled 'Hadhihi Dairat al-Nisa'' (This is the Circle of Women) from the Qur'at al-Khulafa'. The outer square background is dark brown/grey with white cloud-curl corner ornaments, and the concentric rings contain names and verse-directives relating to queries about women — marriage, pregnancy, beauty, domestic matters, female relatives — with the names of female figures or categories in each cell directing the querent to a specific oracle verse. In Islamic oracle literature, the Circle of Women is one of the most commonly included query categories, reflecting the practical use of oracle books for questions about marriage prospects, fertility, and household decisions. The circle format encodes this query category in a visually self-contained diagrammatic form that functions simultaneously as a navigational tool and as a cosmological symbol — the circle representing both the completeness of the classification system and the cyclic nature of fate that oracle literature addresses.

entries.title: Dairat al-Turk (Circle of the Turks) — Qur'at al-Khulafa' (p. 27)
entries.medium: manuscript, ink on paper, gold ground
entries.rights: Public Domain. Princeton University Library (Garrett Collection).
entries.summary: A full-page illuminated concentric-ring circle titled 'Hadhihi Dairat al-Turk' (This is the Circle of the Turks) from the Qur'at al-Khulafa'. The gold-brown outer background with white cloud-curl ornaments frames concentric text rings addressing queries about Turks, Ottoman affairs, armies, military campaigns, and relations with Turkish-speaking peoples. The 'Circle of the Turks' is a query category that would have been especially relevant in the Ottoman context in which this manuscript was likely produced (c. 1700-1835): the Ottoman Empire was the dominant political power in the Islamic world, and questions about military and political relations with the Ottoman ruling class would have been among the most practically pressing queries for users of such an oracle book. The inclusion of the Turks as a named query category (alongside Tribes, Women, Birds, Cities) shows the flexibility of the Qur'a tradition to adapt its query structure to the current political geography of the Islamic world.

entries.title: Dairat al-Ta'ir (Circle of the Bird) — Qur'at al-Khulafa' (p. 33)
entries.medium: manuscript, ink on paper, gold ground
entries.rights: Public Domain. Princeton University Library (Garrett Collection).
entries.summary: A full-page illuminated concentric-ring circle from the Qur'at al-Khulafa', titled 'Hadhihi Dairat al-Ta'ir' (This is the Circle of the Bird) at the top and 'Hakadhaa Dairat al-Ta'ir' (Like this is the Circle of the Bird) at the bottom — the double inscription serving to confirm the circle's identity both before and after it is used in divination. The gold outer square background with white cloud-curl corner ornaments frames concentric text rings addressing queries about birds (symbolic omens, flight divination), but the bird category in Islamic divination also encompasses fortune and fate (as in the expression 'ta'ir' = bird = fate/fortune = the omen drawn from birds). The outer ring contains the names of individual birds or bird-related divination categories; inner rings contain the associated Caliph-oracle directives. The Circle of the Bird connects to the oldest stratum of Arabic divination: pre-Islamic Arabs used bird flight (zayar) and bird calls (siyaha) for omens, and the Qur'a system incorporates this traditional category into its systematic letter-based framework.

entries.title: Dairat al-Mudun (Circle of the Cities) — Qur'at al-Khulafa' (p. 34)
entries.medium: manuscript, ink on paper, gold ground
entries.rights: Public Domain. Princeton University Library (Garrett Collection).
entries.summary: A full-page illuminated concentric-ring circle titled 'Hadhihi Dairat al-Mudun' (This is the Circle of the Cities) from the Qur'at al-Khulafa'. The gold outer square with white cloud-curl ornaments frames concentric text rings listing major Islamic cities (including Baghdad, al-Basra, al-Wasit, al-Mawsil, al-Sham = Syria, al-Fustat = Egypt, and other cities of the medieval Islamic world). Each city cell directs the querent to a specific Caliph oracle verse addressing queries about travel, commerce, residence, or events in that city. The Circle of Cities is particularly evocative of the Abbasid-era geographic imagination: the cities listed are the major urban centers of the 8th–10th century caliphate that the text's poetry evokes, now encoded into a divinatory form that medieval and early modern users could consult about journeys and affairs in those same cities (or their Ottoman-era successors). Baghdad is conspicuously listed — the Abbasid capital — placing it at the center of the divinatory geography just as it was the center of the caliphal state.
